slot.title: Matched grip and the full stroke
slot.lessonGoal: Hold the sticks in matched grip and play a relaxed full stroke that rebounds to its starting height.
objectives: Hold a drumstick in matched grip, with the fulcrum between the thumb and the index finger
Describe a full stroke: the stick starts high, strikes the head, and rebounds to its starting height
Explain why letting the stick rebound keeps the hands relaxed

lesson.title: Matched grip and the full stroke
lesson.lessonGoal: Hold the sticks in matched grip and play a relaxed full stroke that rebounds to its starting height.
objectives: Hold a drumstick in matched grip, with the fulcrum between the thumb and the index finger
Describe a full stroke: the stick starts high, strikes the head, and rebounds to its starting height
Explain that letting the stick rebound naturally and keeping the hands relaxed are both recommended.

blocks.text: How can you hold your sticks without fighting their bounce as you work toward playing “Iris” end to end? You will set up matched grip, locate the fulcrum, and practise a relaxed full stroke that returns to its starting height.

For matched grip, place the stick against the first knuckle of your index finger and put your thumb opposite that point [1]. Keep your thumb parallel to the stick, and curl the remaining fingers loosely around it [1]. Do not squeeze the stick or clench your hand [1].

The fulcrum is the support point between your thumb and index finger [2]. Keep that thumb-and-index contact in place while allowing your wrists and fingers to remain relaxed [3]. The instruction is to maintain contact, not to tighten your whole hand around the stick [3][1].
Use a mirror to check your grip and watch the path of the stick [3]. Can you identify the fulcrum while keeping the rest of your hand relaxed?

blocks.caption: Matched grip places the fulcrum between the thumb and index finger.
blocks.alt: Close-up of matched grip, showing the thumb opposite the index finger at the fulcrum and the remaining fingers curved around the stick.

descriptor.caption: German matched grip on a snare drum: palm facing down, the stick held between thumb and index finger with the other fingers wrapped underneath.
descriptor.alt: Top-down photograph of one hand holding a drumstick over a snare drum head, palm down and knuckles up, the stick angled across the head.

blocks.text: Now check where that contact point sits along the stick by comparing the number of bounces you get at different positions [1]. Begin with about two-thirds of the stick extending in front of your hand [1].

Let the stick drop onto the drum and count its bounces [1]. Move your holding point along the stick, then drop it again and count the bounces at this new position [1]. If you get fewer bounces, try moving your holding point in the opposite direction and compare again [1].

For this test, the recommended fulcrum position is the one that produces the most bounces [1]. You can mark a ring around the stick at that position so you know where to hold it [1]. Once you have found the position, place your thumb opposite the index finger and wrap the other fingers loosely around the stick [1].
What are you comparing during the bounce test, and which result tells you where to hold the stick?

With your grip established, put it into motion: a full stroke starts with the stick raised, strikes the drum, and returns to its original starting height [1]. The return is part of the stroke, not just the downward hit [1].
For one concrete attempt, use your wrist to raise the stick about eight inches above the drum [1]. This gives you a starting height to return to after the strike [1].

Next, send the stick toward the drum and let it rebound naturally after contact [3]. Rebound means the stick’s bounce back upward after the strike [3]. Allow that upward movement rather than stopping it, and return the stick to its original starting point [3][1].
Follow the whole path: high, down to the drum, then back up to the starting height [1]. The movement should remain smooth, without stopping points as the stick travels down and back up [3].
If the stick starts high but finishes low, has it completed the full stroke described here?

blocks.caption: A full stroke travels down to the drum and rebounds to its starting height.
blocks.alt: A sequence showing a raised drumstick moving down to strike the drumhead, then rebounding upward to the same raised position.

descriptor.caption: A full (rebound) stroke in four stills: the stick starts high, falls to strike the drumhead, bounces back up off it, and returns to its starting height.
descriptor.alt: Four side views of a drumstick pivoting at the fulcrum above a drum: raised high, its tip striking the head, bouncing back up with an arrow pointing up, and raised high again level with a dashed starting-height line.

sections.heading: Keep the grip and motion relaxed

blocks.text: Now check the grip and the returning motion together, keeping your fingers, wrists, and forearms free of tension [3]. Maintain the thumb-and-index contact while keeping the wrists and fingers as relaxed as possible [3].
Leave a little space between your palm and the fingers wrapped around the back of the stick [3]. You can also allow some room between your index and middle fingers if that helps your hand relax [3].

Imagine watching yourself in a mirror and noticing that you stop the stick halfway back up. Compare that imagined attempt with the recommended motion: the stick should travel down and back up without a stopping point [3]. Check your arms, wrists, hands, and fingers for tension while you watch the movement [3].

Take your time and practise slowly, paying attention to the small details of the grip and stroke [1]. Use the mirror to monitor both your grip and the stick’s path, rather than watching only the moment of contact with the drum [3].
Can you keep the thumb-and-index contact, relaxed fingers, and an uninterrupted return in the same stroke?

In matched grip, place the thumb opposite the index finger and wrap the remaining fingers loosely around the stick [1]. A full stroke begins high, strikes the drum, and returns to its starting height [1]. Let the stick rebound naturally, keep its path smooth, and keep your hands and wrists relaxed [3].
